# Bonart fixes impact variance and leaves execution cost to calibration

Diffusive realized and counterfactual prices require white impact for information-neutral traders, while the all-pass filter governing decay remains free.

A desk using one impact kernel across every strategy probably has an internally inconsistent model, according to Bonart's paper. For a practitioner, that challenge matters more than the square-root law derived along the way.

## Why must each trader's impact be white?

Bonart defines a trader's impact j as the difference between realized return and counterfactual return, the return that would have printed without the trader: x = y + j. Both x and y must be diffusive: their autocovariance must be a spike at lag zero. Subtracting those conditions yields R_yj + R_jy + R_jj = Δt(σX² − σY²)δ[t]. The paper calls a trader information-neutral when its flow carries no information about y, so R_jy = 0. In that regime, the identity requires R_jj to be white. The trader's impact increments must be serially uncorrelated regardless of how its orders are autocorrelated.

The departure from earlier work is where Bonart applies the condition. Standard models in economics stress the role of intelligent agents who maximize utility. However, there may be situations where, for some purposes, constraints imposed by market institutions dominate intelligent agent behavior. We use data from the London Stock Exchange to test a simple model in which zero intelligence agents place orders to trade at random. The model treats the statistical mechanics of order placement, price formation, and the accumulation of revealed supply and demand within the context of the continuous double auction, and yields simple laws relating order arrival rates to statistical properties of the market. ###### Abstract

Decomposing impact as the difference between realized and counterfactual returns and requiring both to be diffusive yields an identity that restricts admissible impact scaling at the level of individual participants. This constraint implies the square-root law in the information-neutral regime and a crossover to linear impact under strong informational coupling, consistent with empirical observations. keenable.snippet:
Abstract
Structural price diffusivity explains many empirical regularities of market impact
including the “square-root law” and its crossover to a linear regime for low trading rates
[Bonart, 2026a]. One of its central predictions is that an information-neutral trading
strategy generates a diffusive impact state. We microfound this result in an economy
with a trader and many arbitrageurs who progressively eliminate predictable returns.
Each arbitrageur observes realized returns and a private signal of one component of the
fundamental return. As aggregate private information becomes complete and under
suitable convergence to a stationary limit, the trader’s impact law is of the form j =
U ·w, where w is the innovation in the trading schedule and U is causal all-pass. Impact
returns are therefore white, even though no individual arbitrageur can reconstruct the
underlying trading strategy. We then investigate the economic meaning of the impact
phase. We argue that the U which has minimum distance from the filter L generating
the trade flow is an especially interesting candidate: Trade flow is then minimally
distorted under impact and arbitrage, and it always guarantees positive impact costs.
Under a trader flow generated by a biexponential L (the simplest form allowed in our
model) an interesting result emerges: Impact decline is confined to a narrow band
of 50%–60%, lower than some empirical estimates and quite consistent with others.
More complicated flow models can lead to different decays. Finally, we argue that
in real markets, the impact phase is probably somewhat “distorted” in its long-term
tails which allows for a full relaxation of the impact propagator. The effect is weak,
long-term mean-reversion of the impact state.

# Is price-impact decay statistically identifiable by propagator estimation? Diffusive prices force the inferred kernel to be transient and fine-tuned  
Shunta Fujiwara, Yuki Sato, Kiyoshi Kanazawa  
[q-fin.TR](https://arcxiv.org/category/q-fin.TR)arXiv:2611.10574
## Abstract  
Despite the long memory of market-order flow, price dynamics remain diffusive---a seemingly paradoxical coexistence known in econophysics as the diffusivity puzzle. The propagator model has long been regarded as a promising solution: price impact decays in time, finely balanced against the order-flow memory, and propagators inferred from data have been reported to be consistent with this fine balance. Here we prove a no-go theorem: asymptotic impact decay is not statistically identifiable by propagator estimation, since for diffusive prices the fine-tuned decay is returned whether or not the true impact decays. It rests on universal theorems for the Wiener--Hopf deconvolution by which propagators are inferred under long-memory order flow: (i) the inferred propagator is necessarily transient, even when the true impact is permanent; (ii) under a mild condition, it decays with the fine-balance exponent, fixed by the order-flow autocorrelation alone. The fine-tuned decay is thus a property of the deconvolution, not evidence of impact decay. We demonstrate this with an exactly solvable null model that retains order splitting and the square-root law but whose impact is strictly permanent: the inferred propagator shows an artificial fine-tuned decay although the true impact never decays. Nonlinear propagator estimation, being of Wiener--Hopf type, is subject to the same theorems whenever true metaorders have long memory.

Accurate prediction of the droplet size distributions and the underlying breakup mechanisms is therefore of direct practical importance for assessing the environmental impact of oil spills and designing effective response strategies. While these parameters suffice to characterise single-phase jet breakup (Machicoane et al., 2019), immiscible liquid-liquid systems introduce two additional dimensionless groups, the density ratio and the viscosity ratio , where subscript denotes the continuous phase. At low Reynolds numbers, surface tension drives the classical Rayleigh-Plateau (RP) instability, yielding nearly monodisperse droplets whose size is governed by the most amplified capillary wavelength (Rayleigh, 1878; Saito et al., 2017; Sharma et al., 2025b). At high Reynolds numbers, Kelvin-Helmholtz (KH) instabilities dominate the shear layer, driving a turbulent atomisation cascade that produces a highly polydisperse droplet population. parallel-fast.snippet:
In a November 2026 working paper (arXiv:2611.10574v1), Fujiwara, Sato, and Kanazawa establish a conditional no-go theorem for reading causal price-impact decay from propagator deconvolution. When prices are diffusive and second-order statistics satisfy stated autocorrelation monotonicity and response-increment regularity assumptions (Eqs. (5)–(9)), Wiener–Hopf inversion forces inferred permanent impact to zero ( G ∞ = 0) and sets tail decay from order-flow persistence β c = (1 − γ) / 2 alone—as O (τ −β c ) when η < β c (with A G > 0 ensured only under an additional nonnegativity condition on response R (τ)) and as τ −β c ln τ at the boundary η = β c —even in a permanent-impact null model and under daily-segmented nonlinear estimation.

The diffusivity puzzle and what propagator models claim

...

First, each trade's impact decays toward zero so long-run permanent impact vanishes ( G ∞ = 0). Second, the propagator kernel—the weight mapping past order signs to prices—decays at a critical exponent β c = (1 − γ) / 2 that offsets order-flow memory. When empirical deconvolutions recover a kernel decaying near τ −β c , studies often cite that slope as evidence of "long-range resilience of liquidity."
Fujiwara, Sato, and Kanazawa (arXiv:2611.10574v1, submitted November 7, 2026, with Supplementary Material dated November 10, 2026; preprint, not yet peer-reviewed) test that inference using statistical identification —asking whether the estimation rule can separate competing mechanisms from the statistics it ingests. Their theorem proves it cannot: under diffusive prices and long-memory order flow, the deconvolved tail cannot distinguish decaying impact from permanent nonlinear impact.

seltz.title: Market Impact Models: From Almgren-Chriss to Causal Machine Learning
seltz.snippet:
**Market impact models** estimate how much the price of an asset moves *because of your own trading*. For any strategy that trades more than a trivial size, impact is usually the largest single component of transaction cost — larger than commissions and often larger than the bid-ask spread — and it is the main reason a backtest with a 2.0 Sharpe ratio can deliver 0.8 live. This article defines market impact, walks through the three classical model families (linear Almgren-Chriss, the square-root law, and transient propagators), explains why recent research reframes impact as a *causal* quantity that machine learning can estimate, and closes with practical rules for using impact models in algo trading.

## Table of Contents

- What Is Market Impact?
- How It Works: Three Classical Model Families
- Why Regression Gets Impact Wrong: The Causal View
- Practical Considerations in Algo Trading
- Conclusion
- References & Further Reading

## What Is Market Impact?

Market impact is the difference between the price path observed while an order is executed and the price path that *would have occurred had the order never been sent*. Formally, for a parent order of QQ shares executed over [0,T][0, T], impact at time tt is

I(t)=E[Pt∣trade]−E[Pt∣no trade].I(t) = \mathbb{E}\left[P_t \mid \text{trade}\right] - \mathbb{E}\left[P_t \mid \text{no trade}\right].

The second term is a counterfactual: it can never be observed directly. Everything that makes impact modeling hard follows from that single fact. Practitioners therefore split impact into two parts. **Temporary impact** is the premium paid to consume liquidity right now and decays once trading stops. **Permanent impact** is the part of the move that persists, usually interpreted as information the market infers from the order flow.

Abstract

In this article we revisit the classic problem of tatonnement in price formation from a microstructure point of view, reviewing a recent body of theoretical and empirical work explaining how fluctuations in supply and demand are slowly incorporated into prices. Because revealed market liquidity is extremely low, large orders to buy or sell can only be traded incrementally, over periods of time as long as months. As a result order flow is a highly persistent long-memory process. Maintaining compatibility with market efficiency has profound consequences on price formation, on the dynamics of liquidity, and on the nature of impact. We review a body of theory that makes detailed quantitative predictions about the volume and time dependence of market impact, the bid-ask spread, order book dynamics, and volatility. Comparisons to data yield some encouraging successes. This framework suggests a novel interpretation of financial information, in which agents are at best only weakly informed and all have a similar and extremely noisy impact on prices. Most of the processed information appears to come from supply and demand itself, rather than from external news. The ideas reviewed here are relevant to market microstructure regulation, agent-based models, cost-optimal execution strategies, and understanding market ecologies.

seltz.snippet:
Take any conserved stuff — heat, dissolved dye, the probability of finding a jittering particle — and let it flow down its own gradient. Two ideas, stacked, give one equation. The first is bookkeeping: whatever leaves a small region must show up as flux through its walls, the continuity law ut+∇ ⁣⋅J=0u_t+
abla\!\cdot\mathbf{J}=0. The second is a constitutive guess, older than either Fourier or Fick: the flux points downhill and is proportional to the steepness, J=−κ∇u\mathbf{J}=-\kappa
abla u. Put them together and the flux drops out, leaving ut=κ∇2uu_t=\kappa
abla^2 u — the heat, or diffusion, equation. Here uu is a temperature, a concentration, or a probability density; κ>0\kappa>0 is the diffusivity, measured in m2 s−1\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}, and its very units already whisper the punchline: length squared per time, so distance spreads as the square root of time. In the classification of second-order PDEs this is the canonical *parabolic* case — its discriminant vanishes — and that single algebraic fact fixes its whole personality. It runs one way in time, needs exactly one initial condition, smooths its data instantly, and cannot be un-run. It sits between the elliptic Laplace equation (pure steady states) and the hyperbolic wave equation (reversible, finite-speed, two initial conditions). Two solution strategies dominate below: on the open line the Fourier transform diagonalizes ∇2
abla^2 and hands us a Gaussian heat kernel — the fundamental solution; on a bounded domain separation of variables turns the PDE into a Sturm–Liouville eigenproblem whose modes decay exponentially. Both tell one story — fine structure dies first, the whole relaxing toward the harmonic steady state the boundaries demand.

seltz.title: Brownian Motion — Thermodynamics · Fermi
seltz.snippet: A speck of pollen, a fat droplet in milk, a colloidal sphere in water — anything small enough — is bombarded from every side by the thermal motion of the surrounding molecules. On average the impacts cancel, but in any short interval the cancellation is imperfect, and the residual net force jolts the particle along a jagged, unpredictable path. This is Brownian motion: the botanist Robert Brown watched it in 1827 under a microscope and could not explain it; Einstein in 1905, Smoluchowski in 1906, and Langevin in 1908 turned it into the founding calculation of nonequilibrium statistical mechanics and, in doing so, gave the atomic hypothesis its most direct experimental proof. The conceptual leap is that one neither tracks nor needs the ∼1020\sim10^{20} colliding molecules. The particle's coordinate x(t)x(t) is treated as a random variable whose statistics follow from the central limit theorem: the displacement over a time long compared to a molecular collision yet short compared to observation is a sum of many independent kicks, hence Gaussian. The single sharpest consequence is that the mean-square displacement grows *linearly* in time, ⟨[x(t)−x(0)]2⟩=2dDt\langle[x(t)-x(0)]^2\rangle = 2dDt in dd dimensions — the width of the packet spreads as t\sqrt{t}, the fingerprint of a random walk and *not* of ballistic motion. It was this t\sqrt{t} law, not the naive tt of steady drift, that Perrin measured to extract Avogadro's number and settle whether atoms are real. This article owns the phenomenon and the diffusion law ⟨x2⟩=2dDt\langle x^2\rangle=2dDt, together with *why it is linear in time*. It stops there deliberately: the dynamical equation of motion is the Langevin equation, and the identity D=μkBTD=\mu k_BT that fixes the diffusion constant is the Einstein relation — each is its own article. seltz.snippet:
How the Almgren-Chriss optimal execution problem reduces to a Riccati PDE in inventory and time, with a fully computed five-day schedule for a one-million-share order and the TWAP limit.

## PDEs for Optimal Execution Problems

A trader holding one million shares to sell faces a question that no option-pricing model answers: not what the shares are worth, but how fast to let them go. Sell everything in the first hour and the order’s own footprint moves the price against you. Spread it over a week and the price wanders on its own, which may help or hurt. Between those two failure modes sits a control problem whose solution is a partial differential equation in variables that never appear in Black–Scholes.

## 1. The Execution Problem Is Not the Pricing Problem

Every PDE in this series so far has had a price as its unknown and an asset value as its state variable. The Black–Scholes equation asks what a claim is worth given where the underlying is. Optimal execution asks something categorically different: given that a decision has already been made to liquidate a fixed quantity, what is the cheapest path to zero?

The distinction matters because it changes what the PDE is *about*. A pricing PDE propagates a terminal payoff backwards through the risk-neutral measure and produces a number. A control PDE propagates a terminal *constraint* backwards and produces a **feedback rule** — a function that tells you, at any moment, how fast to trade given what you still hold. The output is not a value; it is a policy.

This also means the measure changes. Execution is a real-world problem: the trader bears genuine variance and is compensated for nothing. There is no hedging argument, no replicating portfolio, and therefore no reason to work under the risk-neutral measure at all. Drop a bead of ink into still water and watch the boundary blur. No stirring, no current — yet the dark cloud swells, its edge softening from a sharp line into a smooth halo, until the color fades evenly through the glass. seltz.title: Almgren-Chriss Optimal Execution
seltz.snippet:
**Liquidating a large position is a tradeoff between two costs that pull in opposite directions.** Trade too fast and you crush the price with your own market impact; trade too slow and you expose the unexecuted shares to price risk while the market drifts. The **Almgren-Chriss** model, published in 2000, formalizes this as an optimization problem and produces an *efficient frontier of execution*: for each level of risk aversion, the trade schedule that minimizes expected cost. It is the intellectual backbone of modern implementation-shortfall algorithms and a natural complement to the schedule-based TWAP and VWAP algos. This article derives the intuition, the math, and a Python illustration.

## The execution problem

You hold `X` shares to liquidate over a horizon of `T`, divided into `N` intervals of length `τ = T/N`. Let `xk` be the shares remaining after step `k` (with `x` `0 = X`, `xN = 0`), and `n` `k = x{k-1} − xk` the amount traded in interval `k`. The cost of execution, relative to the arrival (decision) price, is the **implementation shortfall** — the gap between the value you should have realized and what you actually got. Almgren-Chriss models this shortfall as the sum of two impact effects plus volatility risk.

## Temporary vs permanent impact

Market impact splits into two distinct components, and conflating them is a common error:

- **Permanent impact** shifts the equilibrium price and persists for the rest of the liquidation. It is typically modeled as linear in the trade rate: each share you sell permanently depresses the price by `γ` per share. Permanent impact affects *all* remaining shares, so the *total* permanent cost depends only on the total quantity, not the schedule — it is, to first order, unavoidable.

ultimate.title: On Bonart’s interpretation of the Square-Root Impact Law
ultimate.snippet:
Bonart has recently proposed an elegant escape [3]: if realized and counterfactual prices are both diffusive, information-neutral impact must have white increments and the SRIL follows without the wart.

Independently, a volume-conservation argument singles out the square-root law and lays bare the step the diffusivity route must assume: diffusivity fixes the *variance* of impact — an additive, stationary, age-blind quantity — whereas the SRIL is a law for the *mean* impact, which marginally decays as 1/√(age) and therefore demands an origin of time. Finally, the pure all-pass phase left free by diffusivity pins the magnitude of permanent impact to that of the peak, instead of the observed decay toward zero. Together, these point away from whitening and toward a mechanical resolution: the square root reflects *volumes that must balance*, not *correlations that must vanish*.

Finally, Section 6 reframes the diffusivity argument in terms of a purely macroscopic volume-conservation constraint that singles out, but does not pin down, the SRIL. In particular, it makes a clear distinction between the average impact and its standard deviation, which are conflated in Bonart’s argument. The result is suggestive: impact appears to be set by the *volumes* a metaorder must transact, not by the *correlations* it induces.

Real metaorder impact builds up during execution, *peaks* near its end, and then relaxes to a permanent level that is *smaller in magnitude than, and of the same sign as, the peak* — and, for uninformed flow, close to *zero* [15, 8, 9] (but see also [1, 7]). This decay toward a small fraction of the peak is precisely what a pure all-pass cannot produce: its permanent impact is locked at full magnitude, whether at +peak or −peak, and the empirically observed near-zero level sits in the gap between these two poles that the all-pass phase can never reach (Fig. 1).

ultimate.title: Diffusive Market Impact: A Consistent Microfoundation
ultimate.snippet:
Abstract
Structural price diffusivity explains many empirical regularities of market impact
including the “square-root law” and its crossover to a linear regime for low trading rates
[Bonart, 2026a]. One of its central predictions is that an information-neutral trading
strategy generates a diffusive impact state. We microfound this result in an economy
with a trader and many arbitrageurs who progressively eliminate predictable returns.
Each arbitrageur observes realized returns and a private signal of one component of the
fundamental return. As aggregate private information becomes complete and under
suitable convergence to a stationary limit, the trader’s impact law is of the form j =
U ·w, where w is the innovation in the trading schedule and U is causal all-pass. Impact
returns are therefore white, even though no individual arbitrageur can reconstruct the
underlying trading strategy. We then investigate the economic meaning of the impact
phase. We argue that the U which has minimum distance from the filter L generating
the trade flow is an especially interesting candidate: Trade flow is then minimally
distorted under impact and arbitrage, and it always guarantees positive impact costs.
Under a trader flow generated by a biexponential L (the simplest form allowed in our
model) an interesting result emerges: Impact decline is confined to a narrow band
of 50%–60%, lower than some empirical estimates and quite consistent with others.
More complicated flow models can lead to different decays. Finally, we argue that
in real markets, the impact phase is probably somewhat “distorted” in its long-term
tails which allows for a full relaxation of the impact propagator. The effect is weak,
long-term mean-reversion of the impact state.

In Bonart (2026a), I have proposed a framework that rejects this invariance assumption. The starting point is simple: prices are structurally diffusive. ultimate.title: Is price-impact decay statistically identifiable by propagator estimation?Diffusive prices force the inferred kernel to be transient and fine-tuned
ultimate.snippet:
Despite the long memory of market-order flow, price dynamics remain diffusive—a seemingly paradoxical coexistence known in econophysics as the diffusivity puzzle. The propagator model has long been regarded as a promising solution: price impact decays in time, finely balanced against the order-flow memory, and propagators inferred from data have been reported to be consistent with this fine balance. Here we prove a no-go theorem: asymptotic impact decay is not statistically identifiable by propagator estimation, since for diffusive prices the fine-tuned decay is returned whether or not the true impact decays. It rests on universal theorems for the Wiener–Hopf deconvolution by which propagators are inferred under long-memory order flow: (i) the inferred propagator is necessarily transient, even when the true impact is permanent; (ii) under a mild condition, it decays with the fine-balance exponent, fixed by the order-flow autocorrelation alone. The fine-tuned decay is thus a property of the deconvolution, not evidence of impact decay. We demonstrate this with an exactly solvable null model that retains order splitting and the square-root law but whose impact is strictly permanent: the inferred propagator shows an artificial fine-tuned decay although the true impact never decays. Nonlinear propagator estimation, being of Wiener–Hopf type, is subject to the same theorems whenever true metaorders have long memory.

The two competing pictures are separated not by the presence of impact decay but by whether the permanent component of impact vanishes: it is non-zero in the SFK class and it is zero in the fine-tuned transient picture. Our theorems force 𝒢_∞=0 in both classes, so the deconvolution cannot decide which class generated the data.
